name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
summary: Level-order graph traversal exploring all neighboring nodes at present depth before moving to nodes at next depth level.
description: Breadth-First Search is a fundamental graph traversal algorithm. It begins at a starting node and explores all adjacent nodes at the current distance level using a FIFO queue before proceeding to nodes at deeper distance levels. Computes unweighted shortest paths.
problem: Finding unweighted shortest paths and exploring graph level sets in systematic order.
solution: Use a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue data structure and visited state set.

cons: High memory consumption O(V) for wide graphs with large branching factors

name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
summary: Recursive graph traversal exploring as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.
description: Depth-First Search traverses a graph by exploring deeper along each branch until reaching a leaf node or visited vertex, then backtracks using a LIFO stack or recursive call stack.
problem: Cycle detection, topological ordering, and exploring deep branch paths in graph topologies.
solution: Use a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack or call stack recursion with visited set tracking.

pros: Lower memory footprint for deep linear graph structures
Foundation for topological sort and SCC algorithms
cons: Does not guarantee shortest path in unweighted graphs

name: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
summary: Greedy single-source shortest path algorithm for graphs with non-negative edge weights using a priority queue.
description: Dijkstra's algorithm solves single-source shortest path problems on non-negative weighted graphs. Maintains tentative distance estimates and repeatedly relaxes edges from unvisited nodes with minimal tentative distance using a min-heap priority queue.
math: Time: O((V + E) log V), Space: O(V)
problem: Finding minimal weight paths between nodes in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.
solution: Greedy relaxation with min-heap priority queue.

pros: Optimal single-source shortest path for non-negative weights
Efficient O((V + E) log V) with min-heap
cons: Fails or loops infinitely on graphs containing negative edge weights

papers: A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs (Dijkstra, 1959)

name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
summary: Single-source shortest path algorithm supporting negative edge weights and negative cycle detection.
description: The Bellman-Ford algorithm computes single-source shortest paths by relaxing all graph edges V-1 times. A V-th iteration detects negative weight cycles.
problem: Shortest path determination in graphs containing negative edge weights or financial arbitrage loops.
solution: Relax all graph edges |V|-1 times repeatedly; check |V|-th pass for negative cycle detection.

cons: Slower time complexity O(V * E) compared to Dijkstra

name: A* (A-Star) Search Algorithm
summary: Heuristically-guided pathfinding algorithm extending Dijkstra using target distance estimates f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
description: A* search combines greedy best-first search and Dijkstra's algorithm. It selects paths by minimizing f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the exact cost from start to n, and h(n) is an admissible heuristic estimate from n to goal.
problem: Efficient spatial pathfinding and game grid navigation without exploring irrelevant graph regions.
solution: Incorporate admissible heuristic estimation into priority queue scoring.

pros: Significantly fewer explored nodes than Dijkstra
Optimal path guaranteed with admissible heuristic
cons: High memory usage for large state spaces

papers: A Formal Basis for Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths (Hart et al., 1968)

name: Topological Sort (Kahn's & DFS)
summary: Linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that every directed edge u -> v comes before v.
description: Topological sorting orders vertices in a DAG such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u appears before v in the ordering. Crucial for build systems, task scheduling, and neural network DAG compilation.
problem: Ordering dependent compilation tasks or layer execution sequences in directed acyclic graphs.
solution: In-degree array reduction queue (Kahn's) or post-order DFS stack traversal.

cons: Only valid for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)

name: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)
summary: Data structure tracking partitioned sets with near-constant time O(alpha(N)) Find and Union operations.
description: Union-Find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets. Incorporates path compression and rank heuristics to achieve near-constant amortized time complexity O(alpha(N)) per query.
math: Time: O(alpha(N)) per query via Path Compression & Rank
problem: Dynamic connectivity queries and cycle detection in undirected graphs.
solution: Tree representation with path compression (pointing nodes to root) and union by rank.

cons: Does not support element deletion or set split operations easily

papers: Fast Algorithms for Disjoint Set Union (Tarjan, 1975)

name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal & Prim)
summary: Greedy algorithms finding a subset of edges connecting all vertices with minimum total weight.
description: Minimum Spanning Tree algorithms (Kruskal's using Union-Find edge sorting and Prim's using min-heap vertex expansion) find an acyclic edge subset spanning all vertices with minimal cumulative weight.
math: Kruskal: O(E log E), Prim: O((V + E) log V)
problem: Connecting network nodes or wiring layouts with minimal cumulative cost without cycles.
solution: Greedy edge selection via Union-Find (Kruskal) or priority queue vertex relaxation (Prim).
papers: On the Shortest Spanning Subtree of a Graph (Kruskal, 1956)

name: Strongly Connected Components (Tarjan & Kosaraju)
summary: DFS-based algorithms partitioning a directed graph into maximal strongly connected subgraphs.
description: Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) are maximal subgraphs in directed graphs where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex. Tarjan's algorithm uses DFS node low-link values and a stack to find all SCCs in a single pass.
problem: Decomposing complex cyclic directed graphs into condensed directed acyclic component graphs.
solution: Tarjan's single-pass DFS with low-link values and stack tracking.

pros: Single pass O(V + E) linear time complexity
Condenses cyclic graphs into acyclic DAGs
cons: Requires careful stack and low-link recursion tracking

papers: Depth-First Search and Linear Graph Algorithms (Tarjan, 1972)
